summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kenya. Section 162 of the Penal Code makes carnal knowledge against the order of nature a felony punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, rising to 21 years where the act is committed without consent or where consent is obtained by force, threats, fear of bodily harm or false representations as to the nature of the act. Section 163 punishes an attempt with 7 years, and section 165 punishes acts of gross indecency between males with 5 years. The provisions apply regardless of the nationality of those involved. On 24 May 2019 the High Court declined to declare sections 162 and 165 unconstitutional in Eric Gitari v Attorney General (Petition 150 of 2016); the Court of Appeal hearing was scheduled for May 2026 and no decision is recorded in this inventory.

No Kenyan statute governs gender identity, and there is no codified pathway for legal gender recognition; the UK Home Office country policy note of February 2025 records the same absence. Evidence before the Milimani High Court in Nairobi, delivered 20 May 2026 by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, showed that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans had been refused by civil registration offices, with some applicants spending close to four years' wages on document corrections that never succeeded. That court ruled that Kenyans must be allowed to change gender markers on identification documents. Whether the ruling has been implemented is not sourced here.

On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court found that a transgender Kenyan's rights against torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, to equality and non-discrimination, to dignity, to security of the person and to privacy had been violated, and directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act or, in the alternative, to amend the Intersex Persons Bill 2024. The petition arose from nonconsensual medical procedures and a court-ordered 'gender determination' imposed on the petitioner during incarceration, and the court found that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections. Intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender.

Police contact carries documented risk. A CNN 'A Equals' interactive drawing on 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi records routine police harassment, detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, and on-the-spot extortion demands; the same reporting describes trans Kenyans using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through society. The Kenya Human Rights Commission (2011) and the National Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission (2020–2021) reported routine police harassment, detention in remand beyond the constitutional period without charges, presentation on trumped-up charges, extortion and blackmail for bribes, demands for bribes and sexual favours from men who have sex with men, and rape by state security officers.

Violence against sexual and gender minorities is documented rather than assumed. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's 'Lives on the Line' report of September 2025 is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering October 2023 to September 2024, built with more than 14 community organisations, and it explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence. In December 2024 a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist. The Star's 23 September 2025 coverage of the KHRC report notes that its findings rest on purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, and quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's guarantee of dignity the data 'paints a blunt picture' of documented violence alongside community spaces and awareness work.

Forced anal testing of people accused of same-sex relations was ruled unconstitutional by the Court of Appeal in Mombasa on 22 March 2018, reversing a 2016 High Court decision; the case followed the February 2015 arrest of two men in Kwale County who were subjected to forced anal examinations and HIV and hepatitis B tests at Madaraka Hospital in Mombasa, and a later examination on two men taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 hospital was halted by the Kangundo magistrate court. Compensation in that line of litigation was awarded in 2024.

Custody, health care and everyday facilities present specific exposure. The Kenya National Human Rights Commission reported in April 2012 that police face difficulties deciding whether to detain transgender individuals in male or female cells when arrested, and that transgender people fear using sex-designated bathrooms in entertainment areas for fear of being accused or mistaken of using bathrooms for sexual crimes. The same 2012 report recorded that transgender people cannot access gender reassignment therapy, citing a witness who completed all processes but was declined surgery by Kenyatta National Hospital without reasons and whose appeal to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Board was unsuccessful. It also records that when an opposite-sex partner demanding a sexual relationship discovers the person is not female or male, shouting attracts the public and produces stigma and embarrassment for the transgender person.

Article 45(2) of the Constitution, in force since 27 August 2010, authorises only opposite-sex marriage, so a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no recognised standing, and the state recognises no same-sex relationships. The Children Act 2001 makes homosexual and unmarried couples ineligible to adopt.

There are no explicit statutory protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, although Article 27(4)–(5) non-discrimination provisions are argued to allow claims on those grounds and the government in a May 2012 UN submission agreed with that interpretation. The 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association, allowing LGBTQ organisation registration, and a petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination has been filed. LGBTI civil-society groups may operate, but only within a restrictive civic space; the US State Department's 2010 reporting year recorded that the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya was permitted to register and operate, that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread and caused loss of employment and education, and that in February 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

The Family Protection Bill (file DLS/NA/BILLS/2/18/2023), introduced in 2023 by MP George Peter Opondo Kaluma, would allow 'aggravated homosexuality' to be punished with death, criminalise promotion of LGBTQ+ activity, restrict privacy, assembly and public demonstration, prohibit pride parades, provide for monitoring of private and public spaces, remove LGBTQ+ topics from school curricula and overturn the 2023 Supreme Court association decision; it has remained stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years. In 2010–2012 ICCPR and Universal Periodic Review responses the government stated it would not decriminalise same-sex unions as taboo and culturally unacceptable, while stating that it did not support discrimination in access to services including HIV/AIDS prevention under the 2006 Act.
tangentialFactors:
Two court tracks were unresolved at the time of this inventory. The Court of Appeal hearing in Eric Gitari v Attorney General was scheduled for May 2026 with no decision recorded, so the constitutionality of sections 162 and 165 remains unsettled; and the Family Protection Bill has sat before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years, meaning the death-penalty and anti-association provisions it contains are proposed law, not operative law.

The 20 May 2026 Milimani ruling and the 12 August 2025 Eldoret directive both order state action that this inventory does not evidence as carried out. A traveller should treat them as findings of right rather than as available services: no source here describes a working civil-registration process for gender marker changes, and no source describes the Transgender Protection Rights Act as enacted.

The violence documentation in this inventory is qualitative and purposively sampled. The KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report covers October 2023 to September 2024 and draws on organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision rather than a population sample, and the CNN reporting rests on 26 interviewees in two cities. Neither yields a trans-specific violence rate that can be compared with Kenya's general homicide rate, so no such comparison is offered here. The single dated killing with a judicial outcome in this inventory is the December 2024 sentencing to 50 years' imprisonment for the murder of an LGBTQ activist.

Several claims rest on older reporting and are dated accordingly: the US State Department material is from the 2010 reporting year, the KNCHR testimony on surgery refusal, cell assignment and bathroom fear is from April 2012, and the KHRC police-harassment findings cited are from 2011 with NGLHRC findings from 2020–2021. The most recent documented incidents in this record are the May 2026 court ruling and the September 2025 KHRC report; no later instance of police or vigilante harm is documented here.

Kenya's trajectory is court-driven rather than legislative: forced anal testing was struck down in 2018 with compensation awarded in 2024, association rights were upheld in 2023, trans rights were affirmed in August 2025 and gender marker changes were ordered in May 2026, while the Penal Code sections themselves remain in force and a private member's bill pushing in the opposite direction remains pending.

Kenyan citizens bear the full weight of sections 162, 163 and 165 of the Penal Code, which apply regardless of nationality but are enforced against residents who cannot relocate. Community organisations document that police harassment, detention on pretexts and on-the-spot extortion are the routine form of contact: the CNN reporting from Mombasa and Nairobi records cash demands, and the KHRC 2011 and NGLHRC 2020–2021 findings add detention in remand beyond the constitutional period without charges, trumped-up charges, blackmail, demands for sexual favours from men who have sex with men, and rape by state security officers.

Before the 20 May 2026 ruling, 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices and some spent nearly four years' wages on failed corrections; Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition. The April 2012 KNCHR report records that gender reassignment therapy is inaccessible, that Kenyatta National Hospital declined surgery without reasons and that the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Board rejected the resulting appeal.

Employment, education and public life carry documented discrimination. The US State Department's 2010 reporting year recorded widespread societal discrimination based on sexual orientation causing loss of employment and education, and the February 2010 demand by Mtwapa religious leaders for the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute illustrates the local pressure applied to services associated with LGBTI people. outOfScopeNotes:
Implementation of the 20 May 2026 Milimani ruling on gender markers, and of the 12 August 2025 Eldoret directive to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act or amend the Intersex Persons Bill 2024, is unresolved in this inventory. No source states whether civil registration offices have begun processing changes, whether the Act has been drafted, or what remedies exist for a refusal.

The status of the Court of Appeal in Eric Gitari v Attorney General is unresolved: the hearing was scheduled for May 2026 and no judgment is recorded here. Whether sections 162 and 165 survive appeal is therefore not sourced.

Whether the Family Protection Bill has advanced beyond the Committee on Social Protection after close to two years is not sourced, and no date is given for its introduction beyond 2023.

The KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report is described here by its scope, method and legal challenge rather than by incident counts; the inventory supplies no figures for the number of violations recorded between October 2023 and September 2024, and no denominator against which any such figure could be read. The same applies to the CNN interview sample of 26 people.

Several claims in this record derive from a Wikipedia article summarising Kenyan LGBT and trans law, including the Penal Code section wording, the 2019 Gitari refusal, the 2018 Court of Appeal anal-testing ruling and the 2012 KNCHR testimony. They are consistent with the other sources cited but have not been checked against primary texts in this pass.

The intersex third-gender recognition is sourced only to the February 2025 UK Home Office note; the statutory instrument or judgment establishing it is not identified here.
